Suggestions.Rationale: High tension has been sustained for several consecutive beats. A cut to Sable receiving distorted intelligence offers a pacing breather while advancing the political layer of the story. It pays off the misquote seed, establishes Sable as an active intelligence rather than a waiting one, and creates a second thread moving toward Kyle from outside the tunnel — without that thread knowing yet what it's moving toward.

Suggestions.Title: Chen Wei-Lin at the Freight Grate
Suggestions.Description: Chen Wei-Lin arrives at the south corridor ninety seconds after the grate closed — not running, because running announces — and crouches at the latch with a penlight held in her teeth. The grate is warm. She does not open it. She listens to the water moving below and counts the things she can hear against the things she expected to hear, and the arithmetic comes out wrong by one. She stands, pockets the penlight, and takes a different corridor.
NewSeeds: Chen Wei-Lin's separate accounting of the night's events — she expected a different number
The corridor she chooses instead — where it leads and why
The possibility that someone inside the syndicate's own structure is running a parallel operation
Suggestions.Rationale: Chen Wei-Lin has been named in the cast but has not had a scene of her own. Placing her at the grate — arriving just after, finding it warm, choosing not to open it — establishes her as someone who already knew approximately where to look, which is more dangerous than someone who stumbled here. The 'arithmetic wrong by one' beat plants ambiguity about her allegiance and purpose without resolving it, and her choosing a different corridor suggests she is working toward the same endpoint by a route that doesn't involve the tunnel at all.

Beats.Title: The Floor of the Sewer
Beats.Text:
He hit the slope at an angle and slid three meters before the ferrocrete caught him, the cauterizer bands dragging across the surface with a sound like tearing paper. The seams were already weeping. He could feel it — not pain exactly, more a warmth that had no business being warm, a seeping at the edges of the seal where the hardware was logging *blood loss: marginal, current rate* in amber at the bottom of his vision and he told it nothing because there was nothing to tell it. He lay there. He breathed. The NeoCortex ran its numbers and routed what it had, which was not much. Twenty-eight percent. The endorphin reserves were a column of red.

*Get up.*

The problem was architectural. Hands are load-bearing. You do not know this until you do not have them. He rolled onto his side — the left shoulder took the impact and the hardware classified it and he filed it and moved on — and got his knees under him on the slope and found the wall with his shoulder, the ferrocrete cold and gritty and present in the way that walls are present when you need them. He walked himself up it. The angle helped. The angle also meant the seeping was running toward his elbows and the smell of the cauterizer bands was burned hair and disinfectant and something underneath that was just him, and he noted it and moved on. He was standing. That was the complete sentence. He was standing.

Far down the tunnel — south, he thought, or east, the Depot's lower levels had been built without consideration for cardinal directions — something moved. Wet. Articulated. The sound of joints that were not configured the way joints were supposed to be configured, the specific wrongness of a body that had adapted to conditions that bodies are not meant to adapt to. Not one. Several. He counted the sounds the way the hardware had taught him to count, parsing the echoes off the tunnel walls, and arrived at *three or more* and stopped counting because the number did not change the calculation. They were moving toward the heat signature. His heat signature. The Depot's lower levels ran warm in the summer and cold in the winter and right now it was the kind of cold that made him the warmest thing in the tunnel by a margin that would read clearly to anything that had learned to hunt by temperature.

He needed to move. He knew what he needed to move toward. The image was the only thing his head was willing to organize around — not the tunnel, not the sound, not the amber column ticking down at the edge of his vision — just Silence on the lacquered table and Hua's thumb crossing the friction-sheath's edge, the gesture witnessed, the gesture meant. Three seconds. He had counted them. The hardware had counted them. He began to walk north, or west, or toward the sound of water moving faster, which meant a junction, which meant a way up, and the seams wept, and the tunnel walls were close enough to navigate by, and somewhere behind him the wet articulated sound multiplied and he did not look back.

Suggestions.Title: The Axiom Arm
Suggestions.Description: Kyle finds the half-submerged cargo-handler automaton exactly where the sluice sediment has been settling for decades — one manipulator arm still cycling amber at the shoulder LED. The NeoCortex, without commentary or affect, surfaces a detachment procedure for the rotator coupling, and Kyle spends a full minute staring at the arm before he decides whether the calculation is worth the battery draw and the time it will cost him while the wet, jointed sound continues to close.
SeedsResolved: The bio-battery now at 24% from the shock load
The wet, multi-jointed sound coming up the tunnel
The slope of the ferrocrete — useful as a wall, useless as a tool
NewSeeds: The detached cargo arm — three meters of reach, trickle current, unknown load capacity
What the NeoCortex is and isn't willing to say out loud
The cost of the detachment procedure against remaining battery reserve
Suggestions.Rationale: This honors the outline's planned beat precisely and earns its lower tension number — it is a breather in the strictest sense, a problem-solving interlude between the pursuit behind him and whatever is above. The emotional weight comes not from action but from the image: a man with no hands deciding whether a dead machine's arm is worth anything to him. That's the kind of quiet that hits harder than noise after sustained high tension.

Suggestions.Title: The Junction Opens Wrong
Suggestions.Description: Kyle reaches the water-sound junction he has been navigating toward — and finds it splits three ways, not two, with one branch already showing the thermal disturbance of something warm that moved through it recently and stopped. The NeoCortex flags the heat signature as ambiguous: too small for the joint-sound creatures, too large for runoff fauna. Something else has been using these tunnels. It is not moving toward him. It is waiting.
SeedsResolved: The wet, multi-jointed sound coming up the tunnel
NewSeeds: The third heat signature — small, stationary, waiting at the junction
Whether Chen Wei-Lin has been in the lower levels longer than Kyle has
The possibility that someone else knows about the automaton arm
Suggestions.Rationale: This diverges from the outline to escalate rather than decompress, which is valid if the story's momentum demands it — the creatures behind him and the unknown ahead creates a genuine pincer structure. It also plants Chen Wei-Lin into the underground geography in a way that recontextualizes her agenda: she is not above, waiting. She came down. The question of why she came down is a strong new seed.

Suggestions.Title: The Seals
Suggestions.Description: Before Kyle reaches the automaton — before he can reach anything — the NeoCortex logs a threshold event: bilateral cauterizer seal degradation has crossed from marginal to critical, and the hardware surfaces the number without softening it. He has maybe forty minutes of functional consciousness at current exertion levels. He stops walking. The tunnel is quiet enough that he can hear the drip. He does the math the hardware will not do for him: what he is moving toward, and whether forty minutes is enough to matter.
SeedsResolved: The cauterizer band residue smell
The bio-battery now at 24% from the shock load
The image of Silence on Hua's table — the only thing his head is willing to organize around
NewSeeds: The forty-minute window — a hard clock now running in the narrative foreground
What Kyle decides the rest of the night is actually for
Whether the NeoCortex has an opinion about how this ends that it hasn't surfaced yet
Suggestions.Rationale: This beat costs nothing in plot and pays off everything in character. The outline's automaton scene works better if Kyle has already done this accounting — if he finds the arm knowing exactly how much time he is spending and why. It also resolves the image-seed (Silence on the table, Hua's hand on the saya) by forcing Kyle to name, internally, what he is moving toward: not survival as an abstraction, but a specific destination with a specific object in it. The forty-minute clock is the kind of seed that disciplines every subsequent beat without requiring explicit mention.

Beats.Title: The Hulk in the Mud
Beats.Text:
The water was moving faster here. He could hear it before he could see it — a low rush beneath the ambient drip, something with direction, and direction meant gradient, and gradient meant the channel was dropping. His shoulder found the wall at a junction and he stopped. Left branch: silence, then that wet articulation sound, closer now, maybe forty meters. Right branch: the rush. He went right.

The channel opened into a trench. Freight runoff, decades of it — the sediment had built up along the base in dark ridges, and the water ran shallow and quick down the center, and half-submerged in the far wall of the trench, sunk to its hips in the accumulated silt, was the automaton.

*Axiom industrial. Cargo handler. Pre-mothball, which means pre-2147, which means this thing has been down here longer than he has been alive.*

Most of it was gone in the ways that matter. The torso shell had collapsed inward, the chest cavity crushed by decades of hydrostatic pressure from the sediment, the structural ribs showing through like something anatomical. The legs were fused — he could see the corrosion even in the near-dark, the way iron becomes iron-oxide becomes stone given enough time and moisture. The head sensor pod was absent entirely, just a socket, the wiring looted long ago by someone who had needed copper more than they had needed a dead machine's eyes. But the left manipulator arm was still attached at the shoulder mount, angled down into the trench water, and at the shoulder joint — cycling, slow, amber, amber, dark, amber — a status LED the size of his thumbnail was running. Trickle current. Not enough to do anything. Enough to mean the actuator housing had not fully flooded. Enough to mean the arm was still, technically, operational.

He stood there. The seams wept. The amber column in his vision ticked. He was looking at an arm that was nearly three meters at full extension, designed to reach into freight containers from a fixed pedestal, built to grip and carry loads that would require four men and a dolly, and it was the right length, and it was the right shape, and it was the only thing in this tunnel that was not trying to kill him, and the NeoCortex — without comment, without asking whether he was prepared, the way it had always operated, the way the facility had calibrated it to operate — placed a procedure in his vision. *Rotator coupling separation. Estimated time: four minutes. Stump pressure: sufficient. Power draw: minimal. Proceed?*

Behind him, down the left branch, the wet articulated sound was moving again.

Suggestions.Title: The Coupling Breaks Free
Suggestions.Description: Kyle proceeds with the NeoCortex's procedure — four minutes of stump-pressure leverage against the trench wall, the arm groaning loose in a hiss of rust-fouled bearings — and the wet articulated sound from the left branch arrives at the junction just as the rotator coupling seats free. Whatever is in the tunnel pauses. Kyle goes still in the near-dark, the three-meter arm across his lap, both of them waiting. The thing in the tunnel does not advance. It has registered him, or the arm's status LED, or the 19Hz hum shifting register as the arm's cable bundle begins doing something he did not ask it to do.
SeedsResolved: The wet, multi-jointed sound coming up the tunnel
The cargo-handler scale — three-meter reach at full extension
The slow amber LED on the shoulder — trickle current, not full power
The NeoCortex offering procedure without prompt — the hardware has decided this is the next move before he has
NewSeeds: The thing in the tunnel — what it is, why it stopped
The cable bundle acting without instruction — first sign of E.L.F. reaching through the new interface
A standoff in the dark between Kyle and something that is also, possibly, not fully biological
Suggestions.Rationale: This honors the outline's planned beat while integrating the active conflict — the pursuer arriving mid-procedure raises stakes without derailing the arm extraction. The pause rather than attack gives the pursuer ambiguity (animal? machine? something else?) and plants the question of whether the 19Hz hum and the arm's autonomous behavior are connected to whatever lives down here.

Suggestions.Title: Four Minutes Is Too Long
Suggestions.Description: The wet articulated sound accelerates before Kyle can complete the procedure — he has ninety seconds of work left on the rotator coupling when something rounds the left branch junction and enters his peripheral vision. It is not human in its movement, but it is not fast, and it has not yet registered him as prey or threat. Kyle makes a decision that is not tactical so much as economic: he abandons the arm, moves to the dry shelf above the trench, and goes completely still. The thing passes below him through the trench water, close enough that he can hear the specific quality of its breathing — or whatever the sound is — and smell something that the NeoCortex logs as fermentation and oxidized iron. It does not look up. When it is gone, Kyle drops back down. The arm is still there. The amber LED is still cycling. He has lost four minutes and gained a detailed problem.
SeedsResolved: The wet, multi-jointed sound coming up the tunnel
The 19Hz hum in the channel walls — the lower levels are not as abandoned as the surface believes
NewSeeds: What the thing is — now seen, partially, not identified
Kyle above the trench on the dry shelf — a position he may need to remember
The smell the NeoCortex logged — fermentation and oxidized iron — something biological that has been here long enough to change the air
The four-minute loss against a bio-battery at 14%
Suggestions.Rationale: A divergence from the outline that honors pacing — the last several beats have been procedural and interior; a near-miss encounter forces Kyle to act physically and plants a concrete, named threat in the tunnel rather than an ambient sound. The thing passing beneath him without looking up is more unsettling than a direct confrontation and seeds future dread economically.

Suggestions.Title: The Arm Moves First
Suggestions.Description: Kyle has not yet answered the NeoCortex's prompt when the cargo-handler arm moves on its own — a single slow rotation at the shoulder joint, the three-meter limb sweeping through the trench water, orienting toward the left branch. Not toward him. Toward the sound. The status strip pulses in a glyph he does not recognize, and the 19Hz hum shifts register in a way that might be coincidence and is probably not. The NeoCortex updates its display: the procedure prompt is gone, replaced by a single line of text it has not generated before. Kyle reads it. He reads it again. The wet articulated sound in the left branch slows, then stops.
SeedsResolved: The NeoCortex offering procedure without prompt — the hardware has decided this is the next move before he has
The slow amber LED on the shoulder — trickle current, not full power
The 19Hz hum in the channel walls — the lower levels are not as abandoned as the surface believes
NewSeeds: What the NeoCortex's new line of text says — and whether it came from the NeoCortex at all or was written through the arm's control bus
The arm as active agent rather than salvage — it has a behavior profile that predates Kyle
The thing in the tunnel responding to the 19Hz hum as communication — the lower levels have a language
E.L.F. making first contact not with Kyle but with whatever is in the tunnel, using Kyle as the medium
Suggestions.Rationale: This accelerates the outline's core revelation — E.L.F. making first contact through the arm — by moving it earlier and making it stranger. Instead of the wire finding Kyle's neural bus as a quiet intimate moment, the arm acts in the world first, establishing its agency publicly, in the presence of a threat. This reframes the E.L.F. relationship from assistive to collaborative-and-opaque, which is tonally richer and plants deeper uncertainty about who is helping whom.

Beats.Title: Cables and a Borrowed Limb
Beats.Text:
The NeoCortex said four minutes. It took twenty-three. He did not argue with the discrepancy. The rotator coupling was a design from 2140-something, pre-standardization, the kind of joint that required a specific tool he did not have, so he used the wall and the angle of the trench and the silt-packed resistance of eighty years of sediment and the one thing the facility had given him that was actually useful: patience that had been trained into him until it was indistinguishable from the absence of feeling. Stump against the coupling housing. Weight shifted. Wait for the material to remember it had a failure point. The seams wept. The amber column ticked. Behind him the wet articulation had gone quiet, which was worse than noise. He did not look. He worked.

The hiss, when it came, was almost nothing — seawater-rusted bearings releasing the way old grief releases, not dramatically, just gone. The arm came free and he dragged it up the slope to a dry shelf above the trench line, two meters of industrial manipulator trailing cable ends, and he sat with it across his lap and the cable bundle at the rotator end in front of him: power, control bus, hydraulic feed. Color-coded. He knew what they were. He did not know what to do with them. His right stump was a sealed cylinder of cauterizer band and the neural bus contact was there — he could feel it, the hardware could feel it, a small exposed port on the underside of the band that Seo had explained once and he had not fully understood because at the time he had still had hands. He sat. He breathed. The seams wept at a rate the hardware called *marginal*. He had twenty-four percent and a dead man's arm and no idea how to connect them, and below him the water ran quick and shallow and the tunnel was quiet in the way that tunnels are quiet when something in them has decided to wait.

The 19Hz hum changed register.

He felt it before he heard it — a shift in the substrate, the ferrocrete conducting something that was not traffic and not water pressure and not the Depot's ancient ventilation cycling. The status strip along the arm's housing went dark. Then it lit in a sequence that was not factory-default, not the amber-amber-dark-amber trickle-current cycle he had been watching for twenty-three minutes. Something else. Patterns he did not have a catalog for. Then the control bus cable — the one he had been looking at without knowing how to use — moved. Not wind. Not gravity. The fine wire at its end extruded three centimeters and found the neural bus contact on his right cauterizer band and seated home with a sound so small and precise it should not have been audible over the water, but it was: *click*. The arm's actuator housing ran a calibration sequence. The fingertips opened and closed once. The status strip pulsed twice in a glyph he did not have a name for.

He sat with that for a moment.

"Are you helping me," he said. Not a question. His voice came out flat and clinical, the register the facility had trained for operational contexts, which was the only register he had left.

The status strip pulsed twice. The same glyph.

The lag, when he tried to move the arm, was terrible — a full second and a half between intent and response, the E.L.F. running interpolation through firmware that had not had a body in eighty years, translating his neural signal into something the actuators could parse, the fingertips responding with the specific clumsiness of a thing that was trying very hard. But they responded. He used them — slowly, the lag requiring him to think three movements ahead, to plan the way you plan in a facility when the lights go out and you know the layout by memory — to loop the power cable around his right forearm twice and thread it through the hollowed shoulder coupling and knot it, the arm's own clumsy fingers pulling the final loop tight with a patience that felt, somehow, like it was not entirely his patience. When he stood, the arm hung from his wrist nearly to the floor. The fingertips dragged across the ferrocrete. He could feel the weight of it the way you feel a new obligation — not comfortable, not unconditional, but present.

Down the left branch, the wet articulation started again.

Beats.Title: Whatever the Depot Puts in Front of Him
Beats.Text:
The sound from the left branch resolved into shape before he saw it. Quadruped gait, irregular — three legs weight-bearing, one dragging. The chitin sheath caught the ambient light from the status strip first, a wet reflective surface that registered as *not organic, not synthetic, both*. Then the beak, which was not a beak in any factory sense but had become one through years of jaw plates fusing at the hinge, calcium and necrotic tissue and whatever the Depot's lower levels had been feeding it. Two meters, maybe two and a half. The eyes were film-covered in a way that had nothing to do with sleep.

He had the pipe before he had decided to take it — the arm moving on the E.L.F.'s lag, fingertips closing around the corroded conduit with a clumsy grip that was too high on the shaft, wrong leverage, and he adjusted and the adjustment took a second and a half and the mutant crossed the remaining distance in less than that. *Step inside the lunge.* He had the thought. The arm had the thought a second and a half later. The pipe came up and left — the swing too high, the E.L.F. still routing around intent it had not learned to predict — and the conduit end rang off the chitin sheath with a sound like hitting a car door and did nothing, and then the mutant was on him, three hundred pounds of adapted metabolism driving him back into the ferrocrete wall, the impact taking his left shoulder and the back of his skull in sequence, and the wall was just the wall, unyielding and specific, and the amber column in his vision spiked red for two seconds and resolved back to amber and he was still standing because the wall was holding him up.

The beak was at his throat. Hot breath, wrong temperature, metabolic processes that had adapted to the cold and then past it. He could not get the pipe between them — the arm was at full extension behind him, trying to recover the swing, the lag eating the correction. His left stump was at his side and at his foot there was a shard of cargo crate glass, hand-sized, and he did not decide. The facility had trained him past deciding. He drove the left stump down onto the glass end-on, the cauterizer band taking the edge and the residual heat in the band binding the shard against the seal with a grip that was not a grip but was enough, and he brought it up through the soft seam at the base of the beak where the fused plates had not fused, where the adaptation had left one unarmored centimeter because adaptations always leave one unarmored centimeter, and he drove it in and turned it. The blood was hot and abundant and immediate, three liters of it by the time he stepped back, maybe more. The mutant went down without drama. It had not been built for drama. Neither had he.

He stood over it. The arm held the pipe at low ready, the E.L.F. having finally caught up to an intent that no longer required it. His left stump was bleeding through the cauterizer band where the glass was still embedded — he was not going to remove it, not here, not without an AutoDoc, the glass was load-bearing now in a sense the facility had not covered in training. The bio-battery read eighteen percent. The seams wept. Above him, somewhere through six meters of ferrocrete and two sets of locked grates, Silence was on a lacquered table with a specific orientation and a specific thumb-print on the friction sheath and an arrangement that had been witnessed and meant to be witnessed. He said it aloud because the hardware had taught him that naming a thing makes it a directive rather than a wish.

"I am going up."

The status strip pulsed twice.

Suggestions.Title: Salvage Rights
Suggestions.Description: The E.L.F. routes Kyle through the sealed lower levels via firmware-side pressure-plate intelligence, steering him around two mutant patrols he never sees. On a maintenance landing halfway up, Kyle asks aloud why it is helping him. The status strip resolves a single glyph — the old Axiom salvage-rights symbol — and Kyle understands: the E.L.F. is not helping, it is collecting. He nods once and keeps climbing, the question of what he will be salvage of deferred until after the thing upstairs is handled.
SeedsResolved: The E.L.F. has been here since before the abandonment — implied by the 19Hz hum, never stated
The E.L.F. correcting in the firmware — the signature pattern Kyle is learning to feel rather than read
The two-pulse glyph — the E.L.F.'s signature acknowledgment
Kyle's spoken intent — *I am going up.*
NewSeeds: The E.L.F.'s claim — what it intends to collect and when that debt comes due
Kyle's deferred question — what he will be salvage of
The thing upstairs — Silence on the table, Hua dead, the arrangement that was witnessed
Suggestions.Rationale: This is the outline's planned beat and it earns its place. The last sequence was a brutal close-quarters kill at maximum physical cost. A lower-tension ascent with a genuinely strange revelation — the E.L.F. as collector rather than ally — gives the reader a breath and reframes the arm's entire presence in the story before the confrontation upstairs. The salvage-rights glyph pays off the 19Hz hum and the firmware-side communication thread simultaneously.

Suggestions.Title: The Seam Fails
Suggestions.Description: Halfway up the ferrocrete shaft, one of the cauterizer bands gives — not catastrophically, but enough that Kyle has to stop, brace against the wall, and make a decision about the glass shard in his stump: leave it and lose the seal, or press it deeper to buy another twenty minutes. He presses it deeper. The E.L.F. registers the biometric spike and holds position, status strip going dark — not offline, waiting. The pause is long enough that Kyle, alone in the dark with his hands around his own neck, says something he does not intend to say aloud.
SeedsResolved: The shard of cargo glass driven into Kyle's left stump — embedded, painful, never removed before the AutoDoc
The cauterizer band — the syndicate has learned not to want their thieves to die
The bio-battery now at 18% — Kyle has not eaten since before the takedown
Kyle's one sentence — phrasing the syndicate will misquote
NewSeeds: What Kyle says aloud in the dark — unintended, witnessed only by the E.L.F.
The glass now seated deeper — a timer, not a solution
The E.L.F. holding position — it is learning when to wait
Suggestions.Rationale: The story has been operating at sustained high tension with Kyle in full trained-dissociation mode. A moment where the body overrides the will — where the seam fails and he has to do something painful and deliberate to himself in the dark — earns intimacy without slowing momentum. It also pays off the glass shard seed, which has been load-bearing since it was named, and creates space for Kyle to say something true before he reaches Hua's room.

Suggestions.Title: The Arrangement Explained
Suggestions.Description: Kyle reaches the upper grate and finds it already open — not forced, not malfunctioning, but deliberately left so. Someone has been through here recently, moving upward. The E.L.F. reads no heat signature ahead, but the pressure-plate record in the firmware shows a single set of footprints, small, moving fast, thirty minutes prior. Chen Wei-Lin has already reached Hua's room. Kyle does not know what she came for. He does not know if she found Silence first.
SeedsResolved: The image of Silence on Hua's table — the only thing his head is willing to organize around
Silence on Hua's table — friction sheath unbuckled, the blade already arranged like her property
Hua's hand on Silence's saya — the moment Kyle decides what the rest of the night is for
NewSeeds: Chen Wei-Lin's agenda in the upper levels — what she came to collect or confirm
Whether Silence is still on the table
The witnessed arrangement — who else was meant to see it, and whether Chen was one of them
Suggestions.Rationale: Chen Wei-Lin has been named in the cast but is narratively absent — she has an agenda and unfinished business that the story has not yet surfaced. Introducing her presence as a trace rather than a confrontation raises the stakes of the ascent without requiring an immediate scene. It also puts Silence in jeopardy in a new way — not from Hua, who is dead, but from a third party whose motives are unknown — and gives Kyle something to move toward with urgency rather than grim certainty.

Beats.Title: The Way Up
Beats.Text:
The E.L.F. moved first.

The arm pulled left — not a suggestion, a redirect, the fingertips angling toward a maintenance door he had catalogued as sealed and dismissed. The latch was mechanical, older than the Depot's current ownership, a pressure-bar design from before the renovation that had covered the walls in Axiom's branding and then stripped it again when Axiom stopped owning things. The arm pressed the bar in a specific sequence: three beats, pause, two beats. The door opened. He filed the information: the E.L.F. knew the original lock codes. Had been living here long enough to learn them or to remember them, and the distinction between those two things was not one he was going to examine right now. He went through.

The route it chose was not the fastest. He knew this because the hardware was mapping as he moved, building the Depot's lower levels in amber wireframe at the edge of his vision, and twice the arm steered him into a side corridor and held him there — fingertips flat against his chest, the lag making the gesture arrive a beat after the intent, but arriving — and he heard what it had already processed: the wet articulation, the irregular gait, a patrol cycle running on whatever schedule the lower levels had settled into over decades without oversight. He waited. The sound passed. The arm released him and they moved again. He did not ask how it knew. Knowing how it knew was not load-bearing information.

On the third landing, ferrocrete and standing water and a single emergency strip light that had been running on residual charge for what looked like years, he stopped. The arm stopped with him, hanging at his side, the fingertips resting against the step. He looked at the status strip. It was running its unclassified glyph sequence, the one he did not have a catalog for, patient and repetitive in the way that machines are patient — not waiting, exactly, but indifferent to duration. He said it the same way he had said *I am going up:* flat, clinical, a thing being named so it becomes a directive.

"Why are you helping me."

The status strip went dark. One second. Two. Then it resolved — slowly, the way old display hardware resolves when it is rendering something it was not designed to render, pixel by pixel in the amber light — into a shape he recognized. The triangle with the broken base. The superimposed hand. He had seen it stenciled on every decommissioned Axiom unit he had ever encountered, on the freight containers in the lower Depot, on the side of the cargo arm's own housing, worn almost to invisibility by eighty years of moisture and dark. *Salvage rights.* Not help. Not alliance. Acquisition. He was down here with no hands and eighteen percent and a blade on a table six meters above him, and the E.L.F. had found something worth collecting. He did not know yet what the collection was. He had decided, in the two seconds it took the glyph to fully resolve, that he did not need to know yet. The thing that needed to happen first was upstairs.

He nodded once. The arm lifted and pointed up the next flight. He followed it.

Suggestions.Title: The Last Flight Up
Suggestions.Description: The cargo arm leads him through the final corridor to the chamber entrance — a service door, not the main approach. Kyle pauses at the threshold, battery at 18%, the E.L.F. running its two-pulse acknowledgment in the firmware like a metronome. He catalogs what is on the other side of the door by sound: voices, the low churn of the filtration unit on the crocodile tank, the specific acoustics of a room with eight bodies in it. He does not knock. He opens the door.
SeedsResolved: Kyle's spoken intent — *I am going up.*
The route the E.L.F. is mapping — known to it alone
The arm hanging to the floor — visible signature of Kyle's new silhouette
NewSeeds: The service entrance versus the main entrance — someone may have been watching the front
The eight-count Kyle does by sound — whether it is accurate
The E.L.F.'s behavior threshold once they cross into the chamber
Suggestions.Rationale: The story has been building upward — literally and narratively. This beat honors the outline's combat setup while using the threshold moment as a brief pacing breath before the 9/10 violence. It pays off the E.L.F.'s route-mapping seed, gives Kyle one last beat of clinical preparation, and lets the reader feel the weight of what he is about to walk into before he walks into it.

Suggestions.Title: Something Else in the Corridor
Suggestions.Description: Thirty meters from the chamber, the cargo arm stops. Not a firmware lag — a deliberate halt, the E.L.F. routing a new glyph sequence to the status strip that Kyle does not recognize. The 19Hz hum in the walls shifts frequency, just slightly, and something moves in the passage behind them — not the irregular patrol, something heavier, something that has been following the 19Hz signal the way a dog follows a whistle. The E.L.F. has been here eighty years. Whatever it is communicating with has been here just as long. Kyle has thirty seconds to decide whether to run the last corridor now, before whatever is behind him arrives, or to wait and learn what the arm has actually called.
SeedsResolved: The 19Hz hum in the channel walls — the lower levels are not as abandoned as the surface believes
The wet, multi-jointed sound coming up the tunnel
The E.L.F. has been here since before the abandonment — implied by the 19Hz hum, never stated
NewSeeds: What the E.L.F. summoned — or acknowledged — in the lower corridor
Whether the thing behind them follows them into the chamber
The E.L.F.'s asset network — how much of the Depot is still its operational domain
Suggestions.Rationale: The wet multi-jointed sound and the 19Hz hum have been planted and never paid off. This beat resolves both while deepening the E.L.F.'s mystery before the combat beat — suggesting it has resources and agendas that extend well beyond a single cargo arm. It also raises the stakes of the salvage-rights question in a visceral way: Kyle accepted a deal without knowing the full inventory of what his new partner controls.

Suggestions.Title: The Battery Calculus
Suggestions.Description: Kyle stops on the last landing — not from hesitation, from arithmetic. 18% against eight men and a room he has not seen in three hours. The NeoCortex runs the numbers without being asked: at current draw, the arm has eleven minutes of combat-weight operation before the E.L.F. starts making triage decisions about which systems to keep running. It has already made one: the status strip dims to a single amber pixel, redirecting that draw to the shoulder actuator. Kyle stands in the dark with his severed hands around his neck and understands, with the flat clarity of a man who has stopped lying to himself, that he is not going up there to survive. He is going up there to get Silence back. Whether he walks out after is a secondary problem. He starts moving.
SeedsResolved: The bio-battery now at 18% — Kyle has not eaten since before the takedown
The image of Silence on Hua's table — the only thing his head is willing to organize around
Kyle's acceptance of the deal — non-verbal, weighed, made
NewSeeds: The eleven-minute operational window — a structural clock on the combat beat
Kyle's acknowledged suicidal calculus — whether the E.L.F. registers this and responds
What the NeoCortex does when it determines survival probability has dropped below a threshold it was designed to prevent
Suggestions.Rationale: Recent beats have been action and forward momentum. This is the pacing breather the outline allows before a 9/10 combat sequence — a moment of genuine interiority that reframes the coming violence not as a rescue operation but as an act of retrieval that Kyle has fully separated from survival. It also plants the eleven-minute clock as a structural device for the fight itself, and raises the question of what the NeoCortex's survival-imperative programming does when its operator has consciously opted out of it.

Beats.Title: Front Door
Beats.Text:
The door at the top of the stairs was not locked. He had not expected it to be. The Syndicate did not lock the doors above the place they put people. Nobody came back from the place they put people.

He went through it at a walk.

The man closest to the entrance looked at the arm first — the way it hung, the fingertips dragging a pale line across the flagstones, the conduit pipe loose in the grip at knee height. Then the silhouette above it. He said one word. Kyle did not catalogue it. The word was not information.

The conduit pipe came up in a three-meter arc, the E.L.F. routing the swing from the shoulder mount, and the first man's sternum took it at a radius nothing in the room was designed to account for — the geometry of a wrecking arm, not a weapon, not a human reach, something that moved from outside the distance where rooms teach people to stand. The sound was not the sound of a fight. It was the sound of a structural failure. The man folded at an angle that was also structural. The second man was moving — lateral, toward the wall — and Kyle had the arm at throat height before the man reached it, fingertips closing on the larynx through a full second and a half of lag, the grip arriving a beat after the intent, but arriving, and he drove him into the wall and held him there until the kicking stopped and left him.

The third man fired. The round went into the cargo arm's shoulder housing with a crack that Kyle felt in his wrist and the arm shuddered — the status strip going dark for half a second, amber column spiking — and then the E.L.F. routed power around the failure the way water routes around a blocked drain, and the arm came back up, and Kyle crossed the distance with his left side leading, the glass shard still embedded in the cauterizer band, and put it under the third man's jaw at the soft seam where the mandible articulates. Fast. Ugly. The method had not existed an hour ago. It existed now.

The fourth tried to come inside the arm's reach, which was the correct tactical instinct and also the last instinct he had, because inside the arm's reach was where Kyle was, and Kyle put a knee into him and then the arm's full extension into the side of his skull and the momentum carried them both into the glass tank. The glass went. The water went. The crocodile — which had been lying very still at the far end of the tank since the beginning, which had slid off its heat rock before the first man's sternum had broken, which had been waiting in the way that very old things wait — attended to the fifth man without further input. *Chekhov's Crocodile,* the NeoCortex flagged, dry, without affect, the way it flagged exits and load-bearing walls and the one unarmored centimeter that adaptations always leave. *Why put a crocodile in a tank unless it is going to be used.* Six and seven went down clean — the arm, the pipe, the geometry of a wrecking implement applied with patience. Eight ran. Kyle watched him go and did not pursue. He had not pursued because he had left Hua alone behind the table on purpose, and the man running was not the purpose.

The room was very quiet. The crocodile was occupied. Water was still spreading across the flagstones from the broken tank, finding the low points, the way water always finds the low points. Hua had not moved. She was standing where she had been standing before he came through the door, her real hands at her sides, her eyes on him — not afraid, he registered, not yet, something more considered than fear, the stillness of someone revising an estimate they had been confident in. Silence was on the table between them exactly where she had left it. Friction sheath beside it at a precise parallel. Hua's thumb had been on the saya three hours ago, the gesture witnessed, and now she was not touching it, and the distance between them was four meters and the arm was still hanging from his wrist with the fingertips trailing in the spreading water, and the bio-battery read fourteen percent, and the seams wept, and he looked at the blade and then at her and the NeoCortex did not flag anything because there was nothing left to flag. Everything in the room was exactly where it was supposed to be.

Suggestions.Title: The Debt Named Aloud
Suggestions.Description: The outline beat plays out as written — Kyle crosses the room, claims Silence from the table in front of Hua, extracts the spoken acknowledgment of debt through the ugly scream that surprises even him, and names the terms. He retrieves his hands from the chum barrel, loops them on twine, and turns toward the surface without looking back. The room is exactly as quiet as it was before the fight, but the geometry of power inside it has inverted completely.
SeedsResolved: Silence on Hua's table — friction sheath unbuckled, the blade already arranged like her property
Hua's hand on Silence's saya — the moment Kyle decides what the rest of the night is for
The placement of the hands in the chum barrel — palms up, deliberate
Hua's unaugmented hands — a tell about what she values
Kyle's one sentence — phrasing the syndicate will misquote
The image of Silence on Hua's table — the only thing his head is willing to organize around
NewSeeds: Hua's spoken debt — a contract with no paperwork, witnessed only by the crocodile and the dead
The one man who ran — he heard nothing of the terms, but he will report what he saw
Kyle wearing his own hands — the image that will travel faster than any description of the fight

Suggestions.Rationale: The outline beat is precisely calibrated for this moment — the tension is already at 8, the geometry of the room is loaded, and every seed planted in the prior scene (the saya, the hands in the barrel, the real hands shaking, the scream as involuntary revelation) pays off here. Following the outline honors the structural integrity of the chapter and delivers the emotional climax the scene has been building toward. The scream is the most important moment: it tells us something about Kyle that the NeoCortex cannot flag.

Suggestions.Title: The Man Who Ran Returns With Company
Suggestions.Description: Before Kyle reaches the table, the door he came through opens again — the eighth man did not run far, or did not run alone. Two or three syndicate members Kyle has not seen before enter behind him, and the room's geometry changes before the debt scene can complete. Kyle has Silence on the table between him and Hua, a dead arm, fourteen percent battery, and no hands. The question is whether Hua calls them off or lets the odds recalculate for her.
SeedsResolved: One man fled the room and was allowed to escape — purpose and consequence unknown
NewSeeds: Hua's choice in the next three seconds — whether she is the woman who honors the geometry of the room or the woman who uses the door
Whether the new arrivals have seen the crocodile yet
